module_title: Judiciary, Emergency, and Amendment Provisions: Core Framework
introduction: This foundational level introduces three distinct but highly critical pillars of the Indian Constitution: the integrated judicial system, the extraordinary powers of the State during a crisis (Emergency), and the mechanism to change the Constitution itself (Amendment).

core_concepts.title: The Integrated Judiciary
core_concepts.description: Unlike the USA, India has a single, unified, and integrated judicial system. The Supreme Court (SC) sits at the apex, followed by High Courts (HCs) at the state level, and Subordinate Courts at the district level. A single system of courts enforces both Central and State laws.

core_concepts.title: Three Types of Emergencies (Part XVIII)
core_concepts.description:
The Constitution allows the federal structure to temporarily convert into a unitary one during crises:
1. National Emergency (Article 352): Declared due to war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.
2. State Emergency / President's Rule (Article 356): Imposed when there is a failure of the constitutional machinery in a specific state.
3. Financial Emergency (Article 360): Declared if the financial stability or credit of India is threatened (Never imposed in India so far).

core_concepts.title: Constitutional Amendment (Part XX, Article 368)
core_concepts.description: The Constitution of India is neither completely rigid (like the USA) nor completely flexible (like the UK); it is a synthesis of both. Article 368 grants Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and its procedures. However, this power is not absolute.

core_concepts.title: Independence of the Judiciary
core_concepts.description: To ensure courts can check the Executive and Legislature without fear, the Constitution secures their independence. Judges have a fixed tenure, their salaries are charged on the Consolidated Fund (cannot be voted upon by Parliament), and their conduct cannot be discussed in Parliament except during impeachment.

important_entities.name: Articles 20 and 21 (Emergency Shield)
important_entities.key_fact: The two Fundamental Rights that can NEVER be suspended.
important_entities.significance: A heavily tested fact in all law and civil service exams. During a National Emergency, the President can suspend the right to move courts for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. However, the 44th Amendment Act (1978) mandated that Article 20 (Protection in respect of conviction) and Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty) remain active even during an emergency.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will ask: 'Can a National Emergency be declared on the grounds of internal disturbance?' The answer is **NO**. The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced the vague phrase 'internal disturbance' with the specific term 'armed rebellion' to prevent the misuse of power (as seen during the 1975 emergency).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
To remember the Emergency articles, just add 4: 
National (352) + 4 = State (356) + 4 = Financial (360).

exam_strategy_tips: If a question asks 'Which part of the Constitution deals with amendments?', always select **Part XX (Article 368)**.
